question_text: Despite being an abundantly available metal, X was once more expensive than gold itself, because it never occurs in pure form and is always chemically bonded to other elements, usually oxygen, making extraction extremely difficult. Pure X samples were treated as marvels: the French displayed X bars alongside their crown jewels, Napoleon III reserved a set of X cutlery for his most honored banquet guests, and in 1884, American engineers capped the Washington Monument with a six-pound X pyramid to showcase industrial prowess. This lasted until an Oberlin College chemistry professor, Frank Fanning Jewett, inspired his student Charles Hall with tales of the fortune awaiting whoever could efficiently separate X from oxygen. After years of failed experiments, Hall succeeded in 1886 at age 23. The discovery collapsed X's market value virtually overnight. The spelling split also traces to this era: advertising materials for X dropped the extra vowel, whether by accident or design, and Hall liked the result, permanently adopting X in the U.S. Identify X.

In the 1940s, a scientist named Norbert Wiener needed a name for his new field studying how animals and machines control and communicate with one another. He reached back to an ancient Greek word, a verb describing the person who steers a boat, keeping it on course and correcting its direction. The Romans borrowed this idea wholesale, applying the same root to describe a political term. Over the centuries, consonants softened, but the root survived intact, and is still used in politics today, as X. Identify X.
answer_text: Governance (from the Greek root for steersman, kybernan, the same root behind the word cybernetics)

question_text: On April 28, 1923, Wembley Stadium hosted its very first FA Cup Final, finished just four days earlier, with a capacity of 127,000. But somewhere between 200,000 and 300,000 fans showed up, completely overwhelming the stewards and police on duty. Turnstiles were vaulted, fences were climbed, and the pitch became a sea of humanity as chaos threatened to turn into disaster. X became the unlikely hero of the day, gently and patiently helping push the crowd back like a shepherd handling a flock of sheep. The press was so taken with X that they nicknamed the event the '____ ____ Final'. The official report credited the crowd's actual dispersal to the national anthem being played over the loudspeakers, but newspapers and the FA leaned into the story anyway, romanticizing a near-disaster and reshaping a dangerously unruly mob into a tale of order and discipline. Identify X.
answer_text: Billy the horse (the police horse that helped clear the pitch, giving the match its nickname, the White Horse Final)

question_text: In 1978, a computer scientist turned designer named Scott Kim invented a style of calligraphy, X. Isaac Asimov was so struck by this form that he called Kim 'the Escher of the alphabet,' comparing his work to the Dutch artist famous for staircases that impossibly rise forever. Remarkably, another typographer independently invented the same technique around the same time, without knowing Kim existed. Decades later, a young Dan Brown was introduced to this form by his own father, a math teacher, and became so fascinated that he commissioned his book title in this style, then named his most famous fictional hero directly after the artist. Mathematicians love this style for its playful nod to pattern, and today it's found a surprising second life as tattoo art. Identify X.
answer_text: Ambigrams (Dan Brown's Angels & Demons title was rendered as an ambigram, and his hero Robert Langdon was named after ambigram artist John Langdon)

In 1824, an American sea captain named Benjamin Morrell claimed to have sailed into the Weddell Sea, a region off the northwestern coast of Antarctica that, at the time, was completely unexplored. After three days without being able to take any navigational readings, he reported sighting a landmass teeming with life: thousands of sea-elephants, oceanic birds of every kind, and dozens of seals and sea-leopards. He called this newly 'discovered' land X. The trouble is, this captain had a well-documented reputation for deception, and historians later found that parts of his account were lifted almost word-for-word from another explorer's book. No one has ever been able to relocate this land since; later theories suggest Morrell may have been fooled by an Antarctic mirage, or simply mistook distant icebergs for solid ground, making it a phantom discovery. Identify X.
answer_text: New South Greenland (also known as Morrell's Land), located at approximately 67 degrees 52 minutes S, 44 degrees 11 minutes W

question_text: Olivia Rodrigo's third album, You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love, hit screens on June 12th. She released its lead single, 'Drop Dead,' alongside a music video befitting a pop princess, shot by photographer Petra Collins. The video shows Olivia and two other women playing pink electric guitars inside an ornate, gilded room with crystal chandeliers. What unique distinction does this music video hold?
answer_text: It was the first time a music video has been filmed inside the royal apartments of Versailles.

question_text: On January 27th, in Washington DC, a group of scientists made an announcement that instantly became the darkest measurement in their organization's history. Every year, the scientists reassess the state of the world: nuclear tensions, ongoing wars in Europe and Asia, climate change, biological threats, and a fraying international order. In January, they announced their most alarming setting ever, closer to catastrophe than at any point in history, including the height of the Cold War. What was the announcement?
answer_text: The Doomsday Clock was set to 85 seconds to midnight.
